title: Epidemiology and Prevention of HIV (Including PrEP)

questions.stem: A 27-year-old bisexual man presented with a request for postexposure HIV prophylaxis after sexual intercourse. He had not used barrier protection. He asked for advice about routes of transmission of HIV .
questions.lead_in: What poses the highest risk of HIV transmission?
questions.explanation: Receptive anal intercourse. Receptive anal intercourse carries a significantly higher risk of HIV transmission than any other sexual activity.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q34

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man attended for routine follow up. He was asymptomatic. He was known to have HIV and was taking a fixed-dose regimen of abacavir/dolutegravir/lamivudine He was last screened for STI 6 months previously. He was sexually active, and reported three casual male partners in the previous 3 months. He reported that he discloses his HIV status to partners. He engaged in anal receptive and oral insertive and receptive sex. He used condoms for anal sex most of the time. On examination, his oropharynx was clear. His urogenital examination was without discharge, lymphadenopathy, or unusual skin findings. Rectal examination was performed, and no abnormalities were noted. Investigations: CD4 count 900 cells/mm3 HIV viral load undetectable
questions.lead_in: What screening tests should be performed?

options.text: No screening is recommended at today’s visit. Screen annually
Urine and rectal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, oropharyngeal screening by culture for N. gonorrhoeae plus syphilis serology
Urine, rectal, and oropharyngeal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis
Urine, rectal, and oropharyngeal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis plus syphilis serology
Urine screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis

questions.explanation: Urine and rectal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, oropharyngeal screening by culture for N. gonorrhoeae plus syphilis serology This patient has high risk for exposure to STI. In this case, STI screening is recommended at 3- or 6-month intervals. Screen urethral (urine) and rectal sites by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis . Oropharyngeal screening for C. trachomatis is not recommended. NAAT or culture can be used for oropharyngeal screening for N. gonorrhoeae. Note that some NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae are less sensitive because they cross react with other Neisseria spp. found in the oral environment.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q23

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman attended clinic to discuss her birthing plans. She was 37+5 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She had HIV and was taking tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine and boosted atazanavir and reported full compliance. Investigations: CD4 count 456 cells/μL HIV RNA <40 copies/mL
questions.lead_in: What delivery plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Elective cesarean section at 38 weeks with intravenous zidovudine commenced at least 3 hours prior
Elective cesarean section at 38 weeks with intravenous zidovudine commenced at least 3 hours prior plus single dose nevirapine
Elective cesarean section at 38 weeks without intravenous zidovudine
Spontaneous vaginal delivery provided obstetrically permitted with intravenous zidovudine during labor
Spontaneous vaginal delivery provided obstetrically permitted without intravenous zidovudine during labor

questions.explanation: Spontaneous vaginal delivery provided obstetrically permitted without intravenous zidovudine during labor Intravenous zidovudine should be administered to women with HIV RNA >1000 copies/mL (or unknown HIV RNA) near delivery but is not required for women receiving ART regimens who have HIV RNA ≤1000 copies/mL during late pregnancy and near delivery and no concerns regarding adherence to the ART regimen. Scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks’ gestation (compared to 39 weeks for most indications) is recommended for women who have HIV RNA >1000 copies/mL near delivery. https://aidsinfo.nih.gov/co ntentfiles/lvguidelines/PerinatalGL.pdf
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q22

questions.question: A serodiscordant heterosexual couple is seen in clinic: the female partner is HIV positive with a CD4 count of 580 cells/mm3 and a viral load of 280,000 copies/mL; the male partner is HIV negative.
questions.question_raw: HIV sero-discordant couple (female positive male negative). Cd4. 580 and VL 280,000.

parts.text: What are two benefits of initiating therapy in her?
What can be done to reduce transmission if they want to continue to be sexually active? Name three things and give an approximate efficacy for each.
List factors associated with increased risk of transmission.

parts_raw.text: What are two benefits of initiating therapy in her?
What can be done to reduce transmission if they want to continue to be sexually active? Name three things and give an approximate efficacy for each.
Factors associated with increased risk of transmission

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Individual benefit: suppression of viral replication with ART reduces HIV-related morbidity and mortality and preserves immune function. (2) Prevention benefit: ART started at CD4 350-550 reduced sexual transmission to the uninfected partner by 96%, with no linked transmissions once the viral load is suppressed (U=U).

b) (1) Start ART in her and maintain durable viral suppression - 96% reduction in transmission, negligible (likely zero) risk once suppressed. (2) Correct and consistent latex condom use - approximately 87% effective (range 60%-96%) for heterosexual transmission. (3) Daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine PrEP for the HIV-negative male partner - approximately 75% efficacy in serodiscordant heterosexual couples (Partners PrEP), rising to about 90% with detectable drug levels.

c) High plasma viral load in the source partner (risk rises 2.5-fold per 1-log increase; no transmissions below 1500 copies/mL); acute/primary infection or advanced infection; genital ulcer disease (syphilis, HSV-2) in either partner; non-ulcerative STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia, urethritis, cervicitis, bacterial vaginosis); receptive anal intercourse (highest per-act risk, 138/10,000) and unprotected intercourse; lack of male circumcision (heterosexual men); number of partners and prevalence of HIV in the partner pool.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort quotes condoms 80% and PrEP 99%; Mandell gives condom effectiveness ~87% (60%-96%) and PrEP efficacy ~75% (up to ~90% with detectable drug), so those figures are used instead.

cohort_answer.text:
Decreased transmission to partner; Decreases morbidity and mortality associated with HIV infection; Better CD4 count recovery
Condom use 80%; Pre-exposure prophylaxis (Truvada) 99%; PEP 80%; Initiate ARVs, if undetectable negligible risk, detectable viral load up to 40%. Condomless receptive anal sex is highest risk, second highest IVDU
High viral load; Concurrent STI; Ejaculation; Traumatic sexual encounter

questions.question: An HIV-positive male is not currently on antiretroviral therapy. His CD4 count is 865 cells/mm3 and viral load is 2000 copies/mL. He would like to resume sexual intercourse but wants information about how to be as safe as possible.
questions.question_raw: An HIV positive male is currently not an ARV. His CD4 is 865 and VL 2000. He would like to resume sexual intercourse but wanted information about how to be as safe as possible.

parts.text: Counsel this patient on methods for safer intercourse (three things).

parts_raw.text: Counsel this patient on methods for safer intercourse (3 things).

questions.model_answer: (1) Start ART now and maintain durable virologic suppression - a 96% reduction in sexual transmission, and negligible/zero risk once suppressed (U=U); avoid condomless sex until suppression is confirmed. (2) Correct and consistent use of latex condoms (no natural-skin condoms, no petroleum-based lubricants) - approximately 87% effective. (3) Offer daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine PrEP to his HIV-negative partner (up to 90% protection with good adherence), and screen for and treat sexually transmitted infections in both partners, since genital ulcer disease and non-ulcerative STIs increase infectiousness and susceptibility.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort cites condoms 80% and PrEP 99%; the chapter's figures (condoms ~87%, PrEP ~75%-90%) are used.

cohort_answer.text: Consistent condom use or delay sexual intercourse until fully suppressed (80% effective); PEP 80%; Initiate ARVs immediately 40-99% effective; Pre-exposure ppx for partner (99% for non ivdu, 70% for ivdu); Screen and treat other STIs.

questions.question: A man presents to clinic because he has just had sex with a woman known to be HIV positive.

parts.text: Provide two different regimens for postexposure prophylaxis.
State the duration of postexposure prophylaxis.

Duration of PEP.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Tenofovir DF 300 mg/emtricitabine 200 mg once daily plus dolutegravir 50 mg once daily. (2) Tenofovir DF 300 mg/emtricitabine 200 mg once daily plus raltegravir 400 mg twice daily (alternative: tenofovir/emtricitabine plus darunavir 800 mg with ritonavir 100 mg daily). Start as soon as possible and within 72 hours of exposure.

b) 28 days of antiretroviral therapy, with baseline and follow-up HIV serology.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell gives only the 72-hour window and 28-day course (CDC 2005 nPEP); the specific drug combinations are from CDC nPEP 2016.

cohort_answer.text: DTG/RAL + TDF/FTC within 72 hours; alternative: DRV/r + truvada. || 28 days.

questions.question: An otherwise healthy woman had a recent febrile mononucleosis-like syndrome and is now HIV positive, with a negative test six months ago.
questions.question_raw: Lady otherwise healthy with recent febrile/mononucleosis syndrome and now HIV + with prior negative 6 mth ago

parts.text: Would you recommend treatment?
Her seroconversion has now resolved when she sees you. She has a seronegative partner and they wish to stay together "forever." Give two clinical outcomes that treatment has been shown to improve.
Give three options for transmission prevention to the seronegative male partner with the relative percentage risk reduction of each in isolation.

parts_raw.text: Would you recommend treatment?
Her seroconversion has now resolved when she sees you. She has a seronegative partner and they wish to stay together "forever." Give 2 clinical outcomes that treatment have been shown to improve?
Give 3 options for transmission prevention to sero-negative male partner with the relative % risk reduction of each in isolation.

questions.model_answer:
a) Yes. Treat immediately: ART is recommended for all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count, and acute/recent infection is a condition specifically favouring early initiation.
b) (1) Reduced HIV-related morbidity and mortality with higher CD4 reconstitution (rise of 50-150 cells/mm3 in year 1) and fewer AIDS and non-AIDS events, including less extrapulmonary tuberculosis in HPTN 052. (2) Markedly reduced sexual transmission to her partner.
c) (1) Fully suppressive ART for her (treatment as prevention): 96% reduction in transmission in HPTN 052, and 92% in the serodiscordant-couple observational cohort. (2) Daily oral TDF-emtricitabine PrEP for the partner: 73% reduction in the Partners PrEP serodiscordant-couple study (63% in the Botswana study; 44% overall in MSM, rising to 73% with >=90% adherence). (3) Consistent condom use: approximately 80% reduction. Emphasize that all three are adherence dependent.
questions.beyond_mandell: The condom efficacy estimate (~80%) is from CDC/Cochrane data, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
Would you treat: Yes.
Clinical outcomes: Reduces AIDS related and non-AIDS related morbidity and mortality; Decreases transmission; Improves CD4 recovery.
Transmission prevention options: Viral suppression of infected partner 99% (treatment as prevention) – HPTN 052 + PARTNERS study; PrEP for uninfected partner (95-99%); Condoms 90-95% (when used appropriately)

questions.question: A 28-year-old man sustains a needlestick injury from a used needle belonging to his uncle, who is an injection drug user and shares needles with others.
questions.question_raw:
Q12 (2018)
28M sustains needlestick injury. It was a used needle from his uncle who is an injection drug user and shares needles with others.

parts.text: What is the risk of transmission, assuming he is non-immune and does not receive any interventions, if the uncle is seropositive for the following: hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV?
According to the recommendations, name TWO preferred regimens to minimize transmission of HIV and ONE alternative regimen that can be used.

parts_raw.text: A) What is the risk of transmission, assuming he is non-immune and does not receive any interventions, if the uncle is seropositive for the following: Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV
b) According to the recommendations, name TWO preferred regimens to minimize transmission of HIV and ONE alternative regimen which can be used:

questions.model_answer:
a) Hepatitis B: approximately 30% (6%-30%; up to 60% if source is HBsAg and HBeAg positive, about 25% if HBeAg negative). Hepatitis C: approximately 1.8% (range 0%-7%). HIV: approximately 0.3% after percutaneous needlestick exposure to HIV-infected blood (0.09% for mucous membrane exposure); risk is higher with a hollow-bore needle, visible blood on the device, deep injury, a device previously in a vein or artery, or a source patient with advanced disease.

b) Preferred (28 days): (1) Tenofovir DF 300 mg/emtricitabine 200 mg daily plus dolutegravir 50 mg daily. (2) Tenofovir DF 300 mg/emtricitabine 200 mg daily plus raltegravir 400 mg twice daily. Alternative: tenofovir DF/emtricitabine daily plus darunavir 800 mg with ritonavir 100 mg daily. Start within hours (and within 72 hours), with HIV testing at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 and 6 months.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the HIV percutaneous risk (0.3%) is from this chapter; hepatitis B and C per-exposure risks and the specific PEP regimens come from CDC/USPHS occupational PEP guidance (2013, updated 2018).

cohort_answer.text: Risk: Hepatitis B ~30% (HBsAg+/HBeAg-: 25%; HBsAg+/HBeAg+: 27-62%); Hepatitis C ~3% (1.8%, range 0-7%); HIV 0.3% (hollow bore needlestick 0.23%). Preferred PEP regimens: TDF 300mg + FTC 200mg daily + Raltegravir 400mg BID x28 days; TDF 300mg + FTC 200mg daily + Dolutegravir 50mg daily x28 days (repeat serology at 0,3,6 months). Alternative: TDF 300mg + FTC 200mg daily + Darunavir/Ritonavir daily x28 days

questions.question: A child punctures himself with a lancet/needle used by his diabetic uncle, who is HIV positive and not on antiretroviral therapy and pokes himself twice daily. The child is brought to the emergency department with the finger still bleeding.
questions.question_raw: Kid punctured himself with diabetic uncle who is HIV pos and not on ARV, pokes himself twice daily. Kid is taken to emerg, finger still bleeding.

parts.text: List four risk factors for HIV transmission in this scenario.
What is the risk of transmission?
What would you give the child for postexposure prophylaxis?
How long would the postexposure prophylaxis be given for?

parts_raw.text: 4 risk factors for HIV transmission
What is the risk of transmission?
What would you put the kid for PEP
How long would their PEP be for?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Source is viremic - untreated, not on ART, with a high plasma viral load (transmission risk rises about 2.5-fold per 1-log increase in viral load). (2) Percutaneous injury with a hollow-bore needle (the commonest mechanism of transmission). (3) Device visibly contaminated with fresh blood and previously used for vascular/subcutaneous puncture. (4) Deep injury; also advanced disease in the source (source death within 2 months of exposure) and a large inoculum/short time since use.

b) Approximately 0.3% (about 3 per 1000) after percutaneous exposure to HIV-infected blood; by comparison, mucous membrane exposure carries roughly 0.09%. The real-world risk here is lower still, since the needle was outside the body and blood dries.

c) After wound care and baseline HIV/HBV/HCV testing: weight-based tenofovir DF/emtricitabine plus an integrase inhibitor (dolutegravir or raltegravir), started as soon as possible and within 72 hours, dosed by pediatric weight bands.

d) 28 days, with HIV testing at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC nPEP 2016 supplies the pediatric weight-based regimen and follow-up testing schedule; Mandell provides the 0.3% risk and the 72-hour/28-day rule.

questions.question: A man who has sex with men presents to discuss HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis.
questions.question_raw: MSM

parts.text: List four specific indications for pre-exposure prophylaxis.
You are seeing him every 3 months; name five specific tests you should order.

parts_raw.text: 4 specific indications for PrEP
You are seeing every 3 mos, name 5 specific tests you should order

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Condomless anal sex in the past 6 months plus a bacterial STI (infectious syphilis or rectal gonorrhea/chlamydia) in the past 12 months. (2) Condomless anal sex plus recurrent (more than one) use of non-occupational PEP. (3) Ongoing sexual relationship with an HIV-positive partner with substantial transmission risk (not virologically suppressed, or suppression not confirmed). (4) A high objective risk score (HIRI-MSM score of 11 or greater) with ongoing condomless anal sex.

b) (1) Fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody test. (2) Serum creatinine with eGFR. (3) Syphilis serology. (4) Nucleic acid testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia at all exposed sites (urine/urethral, rectal, pharyngeal). (5) Hepatitis C serology (plus pregnancy test in persons who can become pregnant).
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian PrEP guideline (CMAJ 2017) and CDC PrEP 2021: eligibility criteria, 2-1-1 dosing, and q3-month monitoring panel are guideline content, not in this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: A refugee woman is HIV positive with a viral load of 72,000 copies/mL.
questions.question_raw: Refugee woman, HIV +ve, VL 72,000

parts.text: When should you start her on antiretroviral therapy, and what three regimens are approved to give in pregnancy?
What do you suggest for her intrapartum antiretroviral treatment, and what mode of delivery?
You now have a 6-hour-old neonate and the mother's viral load is now 2700 copies/mL. What antiretroviral regimen do you start and for what planned duration?
What test should you do on the neonate and what is the ideal timing of the test?
In Canada, what kind of feeding is recommended and why?

parts_raw.text: When should you start her on ART and what 3 regimens are approved to give in pregnancy
What do you suggest for her intrapartum antiretroviral treatment and what mode of delivery.
Now you have a 6 hour old neonate, mom's VL is now 2,700. What ART regimen do you start and for what planned duration.
What test should you do on the neonate and what is the ideal timing of the test.
In Canada what kind of feeding is recommended and why?

questions.model_answer:
a) Start ART immediately, at diagnosis, regardless of gestational age, CD4 count or viral load - do not wait for the genotype or HLA-B*5701 result; resistance testing is recommended before initiating therapy in pregnancy but treatment is started empirically and adjusted when it returns. Three appropriate regimens: (1) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine plus dolutegravir 50 mg daily. (2) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine plus raltegravir 400 mg twice daily. (3) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine plus ritonavir-boosted darunavir 600/100 mg twice daily (or boosted atazanavir). Abacavir/lamivudine may replace the tenofovir backbone once HLA-B*5701 is negative. Efavirenz is avoided at conception/first trimester because of neural tube defects, and dolutegravir requires counselling about a possible first-trimester neural tube defect risk.

b) Continue the oral regimen through labour and add intravenous zidovudine, 2 mg/kg loading dose over 1 hour then 1 mg/kg/h until the cord is clamped, because the viral load is >1000 copies/mL. Recommend scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks' gestation for a viral load >1000 copies/mL near delivery.

c) Maternal viral load 2700 copies/mL means high-risk exposure: give presumptive three-drug neonatal therapy started within 6 hours of birth - zidovudine for 6 weeks, lamivudine for 6 weeks, and nevirapine (treatment dose) for the first 2-6 weeks. A commonly used Canadian alternative is zidovudine for 6 weeks plus three doses of nevirapine in the first week.

d) HIV virologic testing by nucleic acid amplification (HIV DNA/RNA PCR), not serology, because maternal antibody persists. For a high-risk infant test within the first 48 hours of life, then at 14-21 days, 1-2 months and 4-6 months.

e) Exclusive formula (replacement) feeding; breastfeeding is not recommended in Canada because safe, affordable, sustainable replacement feeding is available and breast milk transmission risk persists even with maternal viral suppression.
questions.beyond_mandell: Perinatal management (regimen choice in pregnancy, intrapartum IV zidovudine indication, neonatal prophylaxis, infant NAAT timing, infant feeding) follows the HHS Perinatal HIV guidelines and CPS/Canadian guidance; this chapter covers only ART pharmacology and IV zidovudine dosing.

questions.question: Consider pre-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir DF/emtricitabine in men who have sex with men.
questions.question_raw: PrEP with TDF/FTC in the MSM population.

parts.text: Give four indications for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in this population.
Give TWO regimens (as you would describe them to a patient) for pre-exposure prophylaxis in men who have sex with men.

parts_raw.text: Give 4 indications for HIV PrEP in this population
Give TWO regimens (as you would describe them to a patient) for PrEP in MSM

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Condomless anal sex in the past 6 months plus a bacterial STI (infectious syphilis or rectal gonorrhea/chlamydia) in the past 12 months. (2) Condomless anal sex plus recurrent (more than one) use of non-occupational PEP. (3) Ongoing sexual relationship with an HIV-positive partner with substantial transmission risk (not virologically suppressed, or suppression not confirmed). (4) A high objective risk score (HIRI-MSM score of 11 or greater) with ongoing condomless anal sex.

b) (1) Daily dosing: one tablet of tenofovir DF/emtricitabine (300/200 mg) by mouth every day, taken at about the same time each day; start at least 7 days before you rely on it for anal sex, and continue every day. (2) On-demand ("2-1-1") dosing for anal sex only: take 2 tablets 2 to 24 hours before sex, then 1 tablet 24 hours after the first dose, then 1 tablet 24 hours after that; if sex continues, keep taking 1 tablet daily until 2 days after the last sexual encounter.
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian PrEP guideline (CMAJ 2017) and CDC PrEP 2021: eligibility criteria, 2-1-1 dosing, and q3-month monitoring panel are guideline content, not in this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: An HIV-positive man is married to an HIV-negative woman and they wish to conceive.
questions.question_raw: HIV + man married to HIV neg women and wants to have a baby

parts.text: Give two ways to prevent transmission and the percent efficacy of each.
List three factors affecting the transmission rate.
State the risk of transmission for one unprotected sexual encounter.

parts_raw.text: 2 ways to prevent transmission and % efficacy
3 factors affecting transmission rate
transmission for 1 unprotected sex encounter

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Antiretroviral therapy for him with durable virologic suppression - 96% reduction in transmission in the randomized serodiscordant-couples trial, with no linked transmissions and negligible (likely zero) risk once suppressed (U=U); time conception to peak fertility once suppressed. (2) Daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine PrEP for her until his suppression is established - about 75% efficacy overall in heterosexual serodiscordant couples and about 90% among those with detectable drug levels. (Condoms outside of conception attempts are about 87% effective.)

b) (1) His plasma HIV viral load (risk increases 2.5-fold per 1-log rise; no transmissions below 1500 copies/mL) and stage of infection (acute or advanced infection is more infectious). (2) Presence of genital ulcer disease or other sexually transmitted infection in either partner. (3) Type and trauma of the sexual act (anal greater than vaginal greater than oral) and adherence to/uptake of ART, condoms, and circumcision status.

c) About 0.08% per act for receptive penile-vaginal intercourse (8 per 10,000 exposures) and about 0.04% for insertive penile-vaginal intercourse (4 per 10,000) - roughly 1 in 1000 per act, higher with acute infection (up to 1 in 50 coital acts).
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort gives PrEP 99% efficacy; Mandell reports ~75% in heterosexual serodiscordant couples (~90% with detectable drug levels).

cohort_answer.text: Prevention: Suppress his viral load (>99% efficacy); PrEP for wife while VL not suppressed (99%). Factors affecting transmission: Viral load; Compliance with treatment; At risk behaviour (active STI lesions). Transmission for 1 unprotected encounter: 0.1%.

c) Give 3 treatment prevention options for the seronegative male partner with the relative risk reduction %

questions.model_answer:
a) Yes. ART is recommended for all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count, and acute or recent HIV infection is a condition specifically favoring early initiation; same-day initiation is feasible and shortens time to viral suppression.
b) (1) Reduced HIV transmission to the serodiscordant partner (96% reduction with early ART in HPTN 052). (2) Reduced HIV-related morbidity/mortality with higher CD4 counts and fewer AIDS events, including significantly fewer cases of extrapulmonary tuberculosis in the early-ART arm of HPTN 052.
c) (1) ART with viral suppression in the partner with HIV (treatment as prevention): 96% reduction in transmission in HPTN 052 (92% in an observational cohort of serodiscordant couples). (2) Daily oral TDF-emtricitabine pre-exposure prophylaxis: 73% reduction in Partners PrEP and 63% in the Botswana study; 44% overall in the iPrEx trial of MSM/transgender women, rising to 73% in those with >=90% adherence. (3) Daily oral TDF alone as pre-exposure prophylaxis: 62% reduction in HIV incidence in Partners PrEP.
questions.beyond_mandell: Condoms (~80-90%) and voluntary medical male circumcision (~60%, three African RCTs) are additional partner-level options not quantified in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
Yes - acute HIV seroconversion syndrome, should start treatment early
Reduced transmission to partner (treatment as prevention); Reduced AIDS and non-AIDS related morbidity and mortality (START trial)
Viral suppression of partner: 99% RRR (U=U); PrEP for uninfected partner: reduces risk by ~99% when taken daily (66-75% Partners PrEP trial, 62% TDF2 trial); Condoms: 90-95% RRR when used properly; Male circumcision: 60-65% RRR

questions.question: A woman acquires human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection through a new sexual partner. Her CD4 count is 580 cells/mm3 and her viral load is not stated.
questions.question_raw: Woman cheats on partner gets HIV, has CD4 of 580, VL ???

parts.text: Should she be treated? Give two proven reasons to treat.
Her partner is negative. What are three ways to reduce transmission, and the approximate percent reduction for each?

parts_raw.text: Should she be treated? What are 2 reasons to treat, I think they said proven reasons.
Partner is negative, what are 3 ways to reduce transmission and approximate percent reduction?

questions.model_answer:
a) Yes — universal treatment is recommended regardless of CD4 count. (1) Individual benefit: early ART reduces HIV-related morbidity and mortality and preserves/raises CD4 counts (with reduced extrapulmonary tuberculosis in HPTN 052). (2) Public health benefit: treatment as prevention — ART in the partner with HIV reduced transmission by 96% in the randomized HPTN 052 trial (92% in a large observational serodiscordant cohort).
b) (1) Suppressive ART for the partner with HIV (treatment as prevention): approximately 96% reduction. (2) Daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis with TDF-emtricitabine for the HIV-negative partner: approximately 44-73% reduction overall, rising to >90% (73% in participants with ≥90% adherence, 32% if adherence <50%). (3) Consistent condom use: roughly 80% or greater reduction in transmission.
questions.beyond_mandell: Condom efficacy (~80-95% with consistent use) and voluntary medical male circumcision (~60%) are from WHO/CDC data rather than this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Condom use: 80-95% effective when used consistently; Circumcision: 60% reduction in risk; PrEP >90% effective but depending on adherence

questions.question: A patient is being started on HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis.
questions.question_raw: PrEP:

parts.text: What are four indications for pre-exposure prophylaxis?
What are five investigations to obtain every 3 months in patients on pre-exposure prophylaxis?

parts_raw.text: A) What are 4 indications for PrEP?
B) What are 5 investigations to obtain every 3 months in patients on PrEP?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Condomless anal sex in the past 6 months plus a bacterial STI (infectious syphilis or rectal gonorrhea/chlamydia) in the past 12 months. (2) Condomless anal sex plus recurrent (more than one) use of non-occupational PEP. (3) Ongoing sexual relationship with an HIV-positive partner with substantial transmission risk (not virologically suppressed, or suppression not confirmed). (4) A high objective risk score (HIRI-MSM score of 11 or greater) with ongoing condomless anal sex.

b) (1) Fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody test. (2) Serum creatinine with eGFR. (3) Syphilis serology. (4) Nucleic acid testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia at all exposed sites (urine/urethral, rectal, pharyngeal). (5) Hepatitis C serology (plus pregnancy test in persons who can become pregnant).
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian PrEP guideline (CMAJ 2017) and CDC PrEP 2021: eligibility criteria, 2-1-1 dosing, and q3-month monitoring panel are guideline content, not in this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: Pre-exposure prophylaxis is given as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine 300 mg/200 mg.
questions.question_raw: PrEP is done with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate / emtricitabine 300mg / 200 mg.

parts.text: What are four indications for pre-exposure prophylaxis in a man who has sex with men and has condomless anal sex?
Write out two dosing regimens as you would explain them to your patient.

parts_raw.text: What are 4 indications for PrEP in an MSM who has condomless anal sex?
Write out 2 dosing regimens as you would explain them to your patient.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Condomless anal sex in the past 6 months plus a bacterial STI (infectious syphilis or rectal gonorrhea/chlamydia) in the past 12 months. (2) Condomless anal sex plus recurrent (more than one) use of non-occupational PEP. (3) Ongoing sexual relationship with an HIV-positive partner with substantial transmission risk (not virologically suppressed, or suppression not confirmed). (4) A high objective risk score (HIRI-MSM score of 11 or greater) with ongoing condomless anal sex.

b) (1) Daily dosing: one tablet of tenofovir DF/emtricitabine (300/200 mg) by mouth every day, taken at about the same time each day; start at least 7 days before you rely on it for anal sex, and continue every day. (2) On-demand ("2-1-1") dosing for anal sex only: take 2 tablets 2 to 24 hours before sex, then 1 tablet 24 hours after the first dose, then 1 tablet 24 hours after that; if sex continues, keep taking 1 tablet daily until 2 days after the last sexual encounter.
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian PrEP guideline (CMAJ 2017) and CDC PrEP 2021: eligibility criteria, 2-1-1 dosing, and q3-month monitoring panel are guideline content, not in this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: An HIV serodiscordant couple is seen: the woman is HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 580 and a viral load of 280,000 copies/mL, and her male partner is HIV-negative.
questions.question_raw: HIV sero-discordant couple (female +, male -). CD4 580, VL 280K

parts.text: What are two benefits of initiating therapy in her?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 benefits of initiating therapy in her?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Individual benefit: reduced HIV-associated morbidity and mortality (AIDS and serious non-AIDS events) with immediate rather than deferred therapy. (2) Public-health benefit: durable viral suppression essentially eliminates sexual transmission to her HIV-negative partner (U=U), and prevents perinatal transmission if she becomes pregnant.
questions.beyond_mandell: START/TEMPRANO and HPTN 052/PARTNER; DHHS guidelines. Not covered in the pages read.

cohort_answer.text: Reduces HIV associated morbidity and mortality; Reduces HIV transmission to sexual partners and infants

questions.question: An HIV-positive man is married to an HIV-negative woman (serodiscordant couple) and they wish to conceive.
questions.question_raw: HIV sero-discordant couple (male +, female -). HIV+ man married to HIV neg woman and wants to have a baby

parts.text: Give two ways to prevent transmission, with their percentage efficacy.

parts_raw.text: 2 ways to prevent transmission and % efficacy

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Treatment as prevention - fully suppressive ART for the HIV-positive male partner: ART reduced sexual transmission by 96% in the randomized trial of serodiscordant couples, with no linked transmissions once the partner's viral load was suppressed, and zero transmissions in PARTNER among serodiscordant heterosexual and MSM couples (U = U). (2) Daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine PrEP for the HIV-negative female partner: efficacy 75% overall in Partners PrEP, rising to ~90% reduction in those with detectable drug levels (85%+ with adherence of four or more tablets per week).

cohort_answer.text: Treatment as prevention – virtually no sexual transmissions occurred once virally suppressed (HPTN 052, PARTNER 1+2, Opposites Attract); anyone starting ART should use another form of protection for the first 6 months until VL<200; PrEP >90% efficacious

questions.question: An HIV-positive man is married to an HIV-negative woman (serodiscordant couple) and they wish to conceive.
questions.question_raw: HIV sero-discordant couple (male +, female -). HIV+ man married to HIV neg woman and wants to have a baby

parts.text: List three factors affecting the transmission rate.

parts_raw.text: 3 factors affecting transmission rate?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Plasma HIV viral load of the source partner - the strongest predictor; risk rises 2.5-fold for each 10-fold increase in viral load, is highest in acute infection (8.2/1000 coital acts) and advanced disease, and no seroconversions occurred below 1500 copies/mL. (2) Type/route of sexual exposure - per 10,000 exposures: receptive anal 138, insertive anal 11, receptive penile-vaginal 8, insertive penile-vaginal 4; anal > vaginal > oral. (3) Concurrent sexually transmitted infection, particularly genital ulcer disease (syphilis, HSV-2), which increases both infectiousness of the source and susceptibility of the recipient; non-ulcerative STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia, urethritis, cervicitis, BV) also increase risk. (Also relevant: male circumcision reduces heterosexual acquisition by 50%-60% in men.)

cohort_answer.text: Viral load; Adherence; Genital ulcers/STI; Circumcision (if Female +, Man -). Also: Type of sex (anal receptive > insertive anal > receptive vaginal > insertive vaginal >> oral); presence of active STI leads to 2-5x increased risk; barrier protection used

questions.question: A health care worker sustains a needlestick injury from an HIV-positive patient.
questions.question_raw: Needlestick injury from HIV+ patient

parts.text: Name four factors that influence risk of transmission and state whether they increase or decrease risk.

parts_raw.text: A. Name four factors that influence risk of transmission and state whether they increase or decrease risk.

questions.model_answer: a) Average risk after percutaneous exposure to HIV-infected blood is ~0.3% (mucous membrane/cutaneous ~0.09%). (1) Device visibly contaminated with blood - increases risk. (2) Device previously used for insertion into a vein or artery - increases risk. (3) Deep injury - increases risk. (4) Source patient with advanced disease (died within 2 months of the exposure, reflecting high viral load) - increases risk; conversely a source on suppressive ART with an undetectable viral load decreases risk. (Hollow-bore needle percutaneous injury is the commonest mechanism and carries higher risk than a solid/superficial instrument injury.)

cohort_answer.text: Source patient: On treatment - decreased risk; VL suppressed - decreased risk (U=U). Body fluid: true vascular puncture - increased risk; Visible blood on needle - increased risk; Unused needle - decreased risk. Degree of exposure: superficial stick no puncture wound - decreased risk; Hollow bore needles higher risk than solid instruments. CDC case-control study: Deep injury (OR 15); Device visibly contaminated with blood (OR 6.2); Needle placement in vein or artery (OR 4.3); Terminal illness in source patient/AIDS (OR 5.6). Majority injured by hollow bore vs solid needle

questions.question: Outline HIV post-exposure prophylaxis after a needlestick injury.
questions.question_raw: Needlestick

parts.text: Describe HIV post-exposure prophylaxis.

parts_raw.text: A) HIV PEP

questions.model_answer: a) Wash the site with soap and water; confirm a true exposure and assess the source (HIV status and viral load). Baseline testing of the exposed worker for HIV, HBV and HCV. Start antiretroviral PEP as soon as possible, ideally within hours; it is not indicated beyond 72 hours after exposure. Give a 28-day course of combination ART - a preferred regimen is tenofovir/emtricitabine plus an integrase inhibitor (dolutegravir or raltegravir). Counsel that baseline percutaneous risk from HIV-infected blood is ~0.3% (mucous membrane ~0.09%). Follow-up HIV serology at 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months, with barrier precautions in the interim.
questions.beyond_mandell: US PHS/CDC occupational PEP guidance (2013) and Canadian practice supply the specific timing, drug regimen (TDF/FTC plus DTG or RAL) and serologic follow-up schedule; Mandell here gives only the 28-day course, the 72-hour window and the transmission risk figures.

cohort_answer.text: Start antiretrovirals as soon as possible, ideally within 1-4 hours of injury. Prophylaxis not indicated if cannot be initiated within 72 hours. Duration of prophylaxis 28 days. Risk of acquiring HIV from hollow-bore needle with blood from known HIV-seropositive source 0.2-0.5%. PEP options: RAL + TDF/FTC; DTG + TDF/FTC. Risk of transmission ~0.3% (mucosal exposure ~0.03%). Clean wound with soap and water, confirm true exposure, obtain baseline serology (HBV, HCV, HIV), repeat HIV serology at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months

questions.question: A man who has sex with men is being assessed for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis.
questions.question_raw: PrEP.

parts.text: Give four reasons in men who have sex with men to go on pre-exposure prophylaxis.
List five laboratory tests to order every three months.

parts_raw.text: 4 reasons in MSM to go on prep
Labs to order every 3 months (5)

questions.model_answer:
a) Condomless anal sex in the last 6 months plus any one of: (1) infectious syphilis or a bacterial rectal STI, particularly if diagnosed in the preceding 12 months; (2) recurrent use of non-occupational PEP (more than once); (3) an ongoing sexual relationship with an HIV-positive partner who is not virally suppressed; (4) an HIRI-MSM incidence risk index score of 11 or more.
b) (1) HIV testing (4th-generation antigen/antibody assay). (2) Syphilis serology. (3) Gonorrhea and chlamydia NAAT from all exposed sites (pharyngeal, rectal, urine). (4) Serum creatinine/eGFR. (5) Hepatitis serology and pregnancy testing where indicated (hepatitis C serology in ongoing high-risk MSM).
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian PrEP guideline (CMAJ 2017) supplies the specific MSM indications and the q3-month monitoring panel; Mandell covers only PrEP efficacy data and FDA approval of TDF/FTC.

cohort_answer.text: Canadian PrEP guidelines (https://www.cmaj.ca/content/cmaj/suppl/2017/11/21/189.47.E1448.DC1/170494-guide-1-at.pdf): Emtricitabine, TDF. Reasons: Condomless anal sex within last 6 months with any of: infectious syphilis or rectal bacterial STI (particularly if diagnosed in preceding 12 months); recurrent use of non-occupational PEP (more than once); ongoing sexual relationship with HIV positive partner with non-suppressed viral load; high-incidence risk index (HIRI-MSM) risk score >=11. Labs q3 months: HIV, syphilis, C and G testing (depending on sites of sexual activity), Creatinine, pregnancy testing if indicated

questions.question: A man who has sex with men and practises insertive anal intercourse presents to the clinic.
questions.question_raw: A patient with MSM who has insertive anal intercourse presents to the clinic:

parts.text: What are four indications for pre-exposure prophylaxis?
Give two dosing regimens for tenofovir/emtricitabine as you would prescribe in clinic.

parts_raw.text: What are 4 indications for PrEP.
b. 2 dosing regimens for DTG/FTC as you would prescribe in clinic.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) A sexual partner living with HIV who has a detectable viral load. (2) MSM or transgender women with condomless anal sex in the past 6 months and/or a documented bacterial STI (infectious syphilis or rectal gonorrhea/chlamydia). (3) More than one course of non-occupational PEP in the past year. (4) People who inject drugs and share injection equipment (Bangkok Tenofovir Study showed 48.9% efficacy overall, 73.5% with detectable drug levels). Also heterosexuals having condomless sex with a partner at high risk or from a high-prevalence setting.
b) (1) Daily continuous oral tenofovir DF/emtricitabine, one tablet once daily (the FDA-approved regimen; ~85%-90% risk reduction with high adherence). (2) On-demand "2-1-1" event-driven dosing for MSM: 2 tablets 2-24 hours before sex, then 1 tablet 24 hours after the first dose, then 1 tablet 24 hours later.
questions.beyond_mandell: The 2-1-1 event-driven regimen (IPERGAY) and long-acting cabotegravir are outside this chapter; indications follow CDC/Canadian PrEP guidelines. Note the part as written says "DTG/FTC" - dolutegravir/emtricitabine is not a PrEP regimen, and the intended agent is tenofovir/emtricitabine.

cohort_answer.text: a) Any person with a sexual partner with HIV and detectable VL; MSM and transgender women who (last 6 months) engaged in condomless anal sex and/or had documented STI; non-occupational PEP use >1 in past year; heterosexual men with condomless sex with female partners in HIV epidemic region; people who inject drugs and share needles; heterosexual men diagnosed with STI or condomless sex with high-risk partners (sex workers, IVDU). b) TDF/Emtricitabine (can be event driven, 2-1-1 dosing: 2 pills 2-24h before sex, 1 pill 24h after first dose, 1 pill 24h after second dose); TAF/Emtricitabine (daily therapy); Cabotegravir LA (monthly x2, then q2 months).

questions.question: Pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV.

parts.text: Give four indications in men who have sex with men to go on pre-exposure prophylaxis.
List the laboratory tests to order every three months.

parts_raw.text: 4 indications in MSM to go on prep
Labs to order every 3 months

questions.model_answer:
a) Condomless anal sex within the last 6 months plus any of: (1) infectious syphilis or a bacterial rectal STI, especially within the preceding 12 months; (2) recurrent (more than once) use of non-occupational PEP; (3) an ongoing sexual relationship with an HIV-positive partner whose viral load is not suppressed; (4) an HIRI-MSM risk index score of 11 or more.
b) (1) HIV 4th-generation antigen/antibody test (add HIV RNA if acute infection is suspected). (2) Syphilis serology. (3) Gonorrhea and chlamydia NAAT from urine, rectum and pharynx. (4) Serum creatinine/eGFR (at least q6 months, q3 months if age over 50 or renal risk). (5) Pregnancy test where applicable; hepatitis C serology annually or more often in ongoing high-risk MSM.
questions.beyond_mandell: Indications and monitoring intervals come from the Canadian PrEP guideline (CMAJ 2017) and CDC PrEP guidance; Mandell covers efficacy trials only.

cohort_answer.text: HIV PrEP Indications: Cis-men and transgender women with condomless anal sex within last 6 months and any of: a) Infectious syphilis or rectal bacterial STI, particularly if diagnosed in preceding 12 months; b) Recurrent use of non-occupational PEP (more than once); c) Ongoing sexual relationship with HIV positive partner with non-suppressed viral load; d) High-incidence risk index (HIRI-MSM) risk score ≥11. Also PWID within 6 months who report needle sharing. Labs q3 months (CDC): HIV 4th gen Ab/Ag + VL; STIs: syphilis, GC+C; Cr q6 months if age>50, Cr q12 months if age<50. Canada GLs: HIV test, Cr, syphilis, GC+C, pregnancy
